findings.title: Tied crypto providers are picked arbitrarily and no longer fail startup
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts CryptoProviders by order() and, if more than one is found, only debug-logs the rest and returns foundProviders.get(0). The previous hard failure for multiple providers is gone. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so any two of them tie. Stream.sorted is stable, so the winner is whichever ServiceLoader yielded first (classpath order), not a defined preference. ServiceLoader also constructs every provider before the sort, and FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE at the front of the JVM security providers even when that implementation is then ignored. A classpath that contains more than one real provider — previously rejected at startup — can now run with the wrong CryptoProvider (including not actually being in FIPS mode) while FIPS JCA providers may already have been installed globally. Equal top order should still be a startup error.

findings.title: order() is abstract and breaks existing CryptoProvider implementors
findings.body: order() was added as a new abstract method with no default. CryptoProvider is a public SPI. Any implementation not recompiled with this change (downstream forks, custom or test providers, an older provider jar still on the classpath) fails to compile, and at runtime ServiceLoader hits AbstractMethodError when detectProvider calls CryptoProvider::order while sorting. That aborts crypto init and server startup. The same interface already uses default methods for optional behavior (getSupportedKeyStoreTypes, getSupportedRsaKeySizes). order() should default (for example to 0) so older implementors still load and lose to the in-repo providers that return 200.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider
findings.body: CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is specified to return the BouncyCastle or BCFIPS JCA provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the provider of the default keystore type: SUN on Java 8 (JKS) and typically SunJSSE on later JDKs (PKCS12). Neither implements the ciphers, signatures, or BC algorithms callers request from this method. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null in the same situation. A non-null unrelated provider makes null-checks succeed, so Security.addProvider or Signature/Cipher.getInstance(alg, provider) runs against SUN/SunJSSE and throws NoSuchAlgorithmException or silently uses a non-BC implementation. This class is the provider selected for the standalone authz client, so any keycloak-core path that uses getBouncyCastleProvider() is wrong. Return null or throw; do not return the keystore provider.

findings.title: AuthzClient.create can lock the JVM onto the stub crypto provider
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). init only runs detection while the static cryptoProvider field is null; every later init is ignored for the life of the JVM. ServiceLoader is given the authz-client class loader, which always sees AuthzClientCryptoProvider (META-INF/services in this jar, order 100) but does not see providers that are only on a child or thread-context class loader. If create() runs before the server's own CryptoIntegration.init — embedded use, or a test that builds a client before server startup — the process is permanently stuck with AuthzClientCryptoProvider. That implementation throws UnsupportedOperationException for signature, PEM, certificate, cipher, and truststore operations. The new order() preference cannot correct this, because the higher-order provider was never visible to the class loader used for the first init. Creating a client should not freeze the process-wide provider on this stub.

findings.title: ECDSA tests use a P-256 key and never check a real signature
findings.body: The suite builds one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and no ECGenParameterSpec, so the key is the JDK default curve (secp256r1). testES384 and testES512 still sign with that P-256 key while passing algorithm.getSignatureLength() (96 and 132) into the converter. ECDSA r/s width follows the curve order, not the JWS algorithm name, so those tests only round-trip 32-byte coordinates zero-padded to 48 or 66 bytes. They never hit P-384 or P-521 sizes or the long-form DER length path that real ES512 signatures need (sequence content longer than 127 bytes). The only assertion compares two outputs of the same codec (DER to RS to DER to RS). A converter that swaps r and s, or that emits DER which Signature.verify would reject, still passes. Nothing tests that CryptoIntegration prefers a provider with order 200 over AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100), which is the behavior this PR says keeps the testsuite on DefaultCryptoProvider. The new codec and provider selection can be wrong and CI stays green.
